description:

Start with a page that matters to your business, such as a service page, a store category, or a lead form. SEO Site Checkup sells its own plans. This SEOGBTools listing is a separate offer. Check which audits, reports, monitoring options, and usage limits are available before ordering. If you need to review several client sites, ask whether the current offer supports that workload and the export formats your clients expect. SEO Site Checkup features

What is SEO Site Checkup used for?

SEO Site Checkup is an online platform for reviewing website performance and SEO issues. Its official platform lists technical SEO analysis and other tools, with availability depending on the plan. A report can help you identify items to inspect, such as how important pages are described, whether links work, or whether the site's setup makes it difficult for people to use a page.

A solo site owner can use the audit to plan the next few fixes. A freelancer can use it to collect examples before talking with a client. A small agency may use reports to compare the same pages over time. Each workflow should begin with the pages the business relies on rather than every warning a tool can show.

An audit score describes the tool's checks. Review the individual items before deciding that a low score needs immediate work. A slow or broken purchase step can be more important than a formatting warning on a secondary page. If the audit cannot reach a page, check what a signed-out visitor sees and whether the page is supposed to be public.

Select pages that represent your site

Choose a small set of important URLs. A service business can check the homepage, a main service page, and the contact path. A WooCommerce shop can select a category, a product, and a policy page shoppers need before buying. A publisher can compare a current guide and an older article. A homepage check alone may miss issues that affect other templates.

Record the exact address and the date of each test. If a URL redirects, note where it ends. Include the expected result, such as a public product page opening on the preferred address. That information makes it easier to compare a second run after a change. A report for a different URL or template may show different results even if nothing broke.

Write down the customer journey you want to protect. A visitor looking for a quote should be able to read the service details and open the correct form. A shopper should be able to find product information and navigate to the intended category or policy. Keeping that journey in mind helps you decide whether a finding deserves immediate attention.

Check indexability and redirects first

Open the most important URLs and confirm whether they are meant to appear in search. Some pages, such as private account areas and staging previews, have different requirements from public pages. If a public page unexpectedly redirects, returns an error, or has instructions that prevent indexing, record the finding and investigate the cause before changing site settings.

For a site you own, compare the live result with Search Console URL Inspection. Search Console may report information from an earlier crawl, while the audit tool can be seeing a newer version. Note the date and the method you used. If you recently fixed a problem, check the current public page before interpreting an older report as evidence that the fix failed.

If a redirect is intentional, confirm that its destination serves the same need. A product that moved to a new URL should lead shoppers to the appropriate product or category when there is a relevant replacement. A redirect to a broad homepage may leave them unsure where to go. Update important internal links to point to the preferred destination where appropriate.

Review headings, titles, and internal links

Read the title and main heading on each priority page. They should help people understand which product or service they are viewing and how it differs from related pages. If a report flags duplicate titles, open a sample of the URLs and check whether they serve distinct purposes. Different services usually need titles that help a visitor choose the right one.

Follow internal links from the pages you are reviewing. If the audit reports an error, find the source link and open it as a customer would. Save the exact source, link text, and final address. A developer can use that evidence to fix a shared template, while an editor can update a link that appears only in one article or product description.

When adding links, choose destinations that help the reader take the next step. A service page can link to a quote form after explaining what the service covers. A product page can link to delivery details where buyers are comparing options. A guide can link to a relevant category after helping someone choose a size. Reopen the final page and confirm the links are easy to find.

Check performance and usability on a real journey

An audit can point to performance concerns, but it helps to open the page and see what a visitor needs first. On a small screen, check when the main heading, product image, and action become usable. If the most important part of the page feels slow, look for a likely cause such as an oversized image or a layout that changes as other elements load.

If you run performance tests, keep the settings comparable. A single lab result can be affected by the conditions at the time. If you have access to real-user measurements, compare them with the specific issue you observe. Choose a fix you can verify, such as reducing the size of a key image or changing how a nonessential element loads.

Test the action after the change. If a mobile form or checkout link was hard to use, reopen it on a narrow screen. Make sure important text and controls still appear. A better report score is helpful only when the page works for the people who need to use it. Keep a short note of what you actually observed.

Make a fix list that someone can verify

Give each issue a clear title and owner. Record the affected URL, expected behavior, what you found, and how to test the result. A task saying “fix SEO” is difficult to assign. A task saying “update the delivery link in the product template and test it from three live products” gives a developer and reviewer a clear job.

Group related issues. If several pages share a broken menu link, identify the shared navigation rather than opening a separate task for every page. If only one product has a bad link copied into its description, assign that page to the editor. Recheck a sample of affected pages after the fix so you can see whether the same issue appears elsewhere.

Decide what to do when a finding cannot be reproduced. Keep it in a review list with the date and settings used by the audit. If it appears again, compare the new example with the original. Do not promise a fix for a problem you have not observed or linked to the intended behavior.

Example audit for a local service business

Imagine a painting company wants more quote requests from its exterior service page. Run an audit on the page and open it on mobile. If the quote button points to an old form, correct that path before rewriting the whole page. Verify that the new destination opens and that the form explains what the customer needs to provide.

Then read the title and main content. Check whether the page names the service and area accurately and answers questions about surfaces, preparation, and booking where the business can confirm those details. If the same title appears on the interior and exterior pages, give each a distinct purpose and heading. Use a relevant internal link when someone might need the other service.

After publishing the fixes, repeat the mobile journey and rerun the audit for the same URL. Record which issue changed and which items still need work. If the company wants to compare enquiries over time, note promotions and seasonal demand. A working quote link is a verified improvement even before you have enough data to measure the effect on leads.

Compare group buy access and official plans

Check the current price, access period, audit allowances, project limits, and export options. If you need a recurring scan or a report to share with a client, test that exact workflow before relying on it. Ask whether any features on the vendor’s pricing page require a separate plan or are outside the SEOGBTools offer. SEO Site Checkup official pricing

Use a public website for your first test. Choose one URL, run an audit, and record one issue you can reproduce. Check whether you can keep the result in the format your project requires. If a report asks for connected account access or information about a private site, confirm what you are allowed to share before setting it up.

For a second website review workflow, compare SEOptimer Group Buy. If you need to trace internal links across a larger site, see Screaming Frog Group Buy. Test the same problem in each workflow so you can tell which report gives you the evidence you need.

Keep a record of accepted exceptions

Some findings reflect a choice the site owner made. A login page may be excluded from search on purpose. An old URL may redirect because the page moved. Record the decision, who confirmed it, and the date. When the same finding appears in a later report, the next reviewer can tell whether the behavior is expected or whether it needs a new investigation.

For issues that affect a shared template, keep one before and after example for each page type you tested. Open the URLs after a theme or navigation update and repeat the customer task. If the same problem returns, compare the current behavior with the old evidence. This helps the developer identify where the change came from. Give the issue one owner and set a review date when the fix depends on a later release.

Frequently asked questions

Is SEO Site Checkup enough for a full technical audit?

It can help you find issues to investigate. The scope depends on the features available and the site you need to check. Verify important issues directly and use other sources for parts of the audit that need additional evidence.

Which page should I audit first?

Choose a page that matters to sales, enquiries, or organic search. Check the next step a customer takes from it. Once you understand that journey, add examples from other important templates.

How do I know whether an SEO warning needs a fix?

Confirm the behavior on the public page and compare it with the page's purpose. Give priority to issues that affect search visibility or stop visitors from completing an important action.

Can I assume white-label reports or monitoring are included?

Ask about the exact reporting and monitoring features you need. The official plan descriptions and this listing can differ. Verify the report format, site limits, and scheduling before promising it to a client.

When should I rerun a website audit?

Rerun the relevant check after a fix is live. Compare the same URL and scope, and record the date. Review the public page yourself before closing a task based on a new report.
